solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cold broth's served up — being this?

definitions.text: Cold broth's served up — being this?

indicators.note: A dish that is served up has been prepared and plated, so the letters arrive worked into a new arrangement.

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
taken letter for letter, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A waiter admits the soup came out cold and wonders what to call it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the recipe and the description: borscht is a beetroot soup often served chilled, and C plus BROTHS reshuffled spells it.
explanation.definitionFit: Borscht is an Eastern European beetroot broth, commonly eaten cold in summer.

clue.text: What jester often has left to replace deficiency in TV comedy

indicators.note: One piece is told to replace another, so a word in the TV title is swapped out for a new letter.

parts.note: the BBC sitcom starring Rowan Atkinson
a lack is a deficiency; this is the chunk taken out
L is the usual abbreviation for left; it goes in where LACK was

explanation.surface: A description of how a TV comedy's weak spots are patched with jokes about the jester.
explanation.walkthrough: BLACKADDER is a British historical sitcom; swap its LACK for L and B-L-ADDER remains. Court jesters carried a mock sceptre tipped with an inflated animal bladder.
explanation.definitionFit: A jester's bauble was often an inflated pig's bladder on a stick, used for comic thwacking.

clue.text: Scamp reportedly stole onion

indicators.note: What is reported comes by word of mouth, so we want the sound of the word rather than its spelling.

parts.note: a stole is a wrap worn round the shoulders; WRAP and RAP are said the same
a scallion is a spring onion

explanation.surface: A small rascal is said to have pinched an onion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' looks like the verb to go with the scamp's theft; it is the noun, a shawl or WRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapscallion is a mischievous rogue, which is what a scamp is.

clue.text: Plant bay bordering lake and river

indicators.note: Something bordering another forms its edges, so the outer letters wrap round the inner one.

parts.note: a cove is a small bay
L for lake, set inside COVER after the C
R is the map abbreviation for river; COVE + R = COVER

explanation.surface: A gardener is choosing a spot to plant a bay tree near water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant bay' reads as an instruction to put in a bay tree; 'Plant' is the definition and 'bay' is COVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Clover is a low-growing plant of the pea family.

clue.text: Declaring for your information in strange setting

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation goes inside the rearranged letters
strange signals that 'setting' appears in an odd new order

explanation.surface: Making an announcement, just to let you know, in an unusual place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' looks like a place, but it is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To testify is to state something formally as evidence, so testifying is declaring.

clue.text: Notice no longer available to stop work

parts.note: a sign is a posted notice
as a dish on a menu is off when it has run out

explanation.surface: A notice goes up saying something has sold out, bringing work to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' tempts as a verb; it is the noun SIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign off is to finish work for the day, or to end a broadcast.

clue.text: Ledge below window is even now losing temperature

indicators.note: A word losing something has a letter taken away from it.

parts.note: still, as in 'even now'
T for temperature, removed from STILL

explanation.surface: Someone watching the thermometer on a window ledge notices the temperature is still dropping.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the scientific abbreviation for temperature; STILL without it is SILL.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition describes the thing rather than naming a synonym: the ledge at the foot of a window frame has its own word.

clue.text: Note a minor attempt to manipulate

parts.note: G is one of the musical notes A to G
taken as printed
a slight or minor matter

explanation.surface: A memo describes a small effort at manipulation.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase: to gaslight someone is to try to make them doubt their own sense of reality.
explanation.definitionFit: To gaslight is to manipulate someone psychologically, named after the play and film Gas Light.

clue.text: Mineral found in no other mine ultimately

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so take the last letter of each word.

parts.note: the last letters of nO, otheR, minE

explanation.surface: A mineral that turns up only in one particular mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' seems to belong to the mine's story; it points at the final letter of each of the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ore is rock or mineral from which metal is extracted.

clue.text: Note score as one goes down finally?

parts.note: FA is a note in the sol-fa scale (do re mi fa...)
a tally is a score or running count

explanation.surface: A reminder to write down the score as a player falls at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: someone who goes down for the last time, never to rise, has fallen fatally.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatally means in a way that ends in death, the final going down.

clue.text: A record height

parts.note: taken as printed
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: An athlete sets a new best in the high jump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record height' reads as a best-ever mark; 'record' is LP and 'height' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Height' is used in its sense of a high place or summit, and an Alpine mountain is one.

clue.text: Bad smell over aroma of fish past its prime

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the two letters are read backwards

parts.note: BO is body odour, a bad smell
a sole is a flatfish
an aroma is a scent

explanation.surface: A rank smell rising from fish that has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aroma of fish' is read as the fish's aroma, so the fish comes before the aroma in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsolescent means becoming obsolete or outdated, so declining after its best days.

clue.text: Ruling abandoning last mine gone to rack and ruin

indicators.note: abandoning last says the ruling word drops its final letter

parts.note: a decree is an official ruling
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: A judgment closing the final colliery leaves things in ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: Decrepit means worn out and dilapidated through age or neglect, the state of something fallen into ruin.

clue.text: Tax's current range reduced after first of February

definitions.note: an adjective meaning relating to tax, like the possessive

indicators.note: after says the current and range pieces come behind the February letter
first of picks the opening letter of 'February'

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: reduced means the word is shortened by its final letter

parts.note: a scale is a range of values

explanation.surface: The current range of tax rates is cut back after the start of February.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiscal means relating to public revenue and taxation, as in fiscal policy.

clue.text: Guy perhaps gets round concerning brief challenge possible to overcome

indicators.note: gets round says the cable surrounds the following pieces

parts.note: a guy is a rope or cable that holds something steady, so a cable is an example
on means concerning or about

indicators.note: brief means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a query is a question or challenge

explanation.surface: A man called Guy dodges a short challenge about something that can be beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man's name; it is a guy rope, a cable steadying a tent or mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Conquerable means able to be conquered, defeated or overcome.

clue.text: Stupid individual almost decapitated guards

indicators.note: A thing that guards another surrounds it protectively.

parts.note: beheaded means decapitated

indicators.note: 'almost' cuts a letter off

parts.note: ONE is what 'individual' stands for

explanation.surface: A dim-witted person has had the guards nearly lose their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost decapitated' wants to go together; 'almost' belongs to 'individual', and BEHEADED is complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Boneheaded means stupid, as if the skull were solid bone.

clue.text: Narrow channel runs badly

parts.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
ill as in 'ill-treated'

explanation.surface: A narrow channel is performing poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: R for runs comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rill is a small stream or narrow channel of water.

clue.text: Bootlicking — or a less healthy desire, it's said

indicators.note: What is said is heard, not read, so the sound gives the answer.

parts.note: sicker is less healthy and a fancy is a desire

explanation.surface: Grovelling is dismissed as an unhealthy craving.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' is part of the surface only. In a non-rhotic British accent SICKER FANCY and SYCOPHANCY sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Sycophancy is servile flattery, which is what bootlicking is.

clue.text: United sacked Newport City man

parts.note: U for United, as in football team names

indicators.note: A sacked town has been plundered and wrecked, so its letters are left in disorder.

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A football result: United thrashed Newport City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newport City' looks like a club name; 'City man' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An uptowner lives in the uptown part of a city.

clue.text: Being in Africa, I'm with tank unit nearly trapped by revolutionary

indicators.note: trapped by says the pieces are held inside the revolutionary's name

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's stock revolutionary
taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: nearly means the word stops short of its last letter

parts.note: a panzer is a German tank or armoured unit

explanation.surface: A soldier in Africa, part of a tank unit, almost captured by a guerrilla.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a verb but is a noun, a living creature; Che Guevara is the stock revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimpanzee is an ape living in the forests of Africa, so a creature there; 'being' means a living creature.

clue.text: Inception of Charles' reign's overturned in error

indicators.note: The inception is the very start, so take the first letter.

parts.note: the first letter of Charles

indicators.note: Something overturned is upside down, which in a down entry means the letters run backwards.

parts.note: REGNAL, meaning of a reign, turned round

explanation.surface: Starting King Charles's reign turns out to have been a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: REGNAL is the adjective 'relating to a reign', matching the possessive 'reign's'. A clanger is British slang for a glaring blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A clanger is an embarrassing mistake, one that drops noisily.

clue.text: President in black American hearts

parts.note: B for black, as on pencils
US for American
H for hearts, the card suit

explanation.surface: A president wears black with American hearts on his sleeve.
explanation.walkthrough: Either President Bush fits; 'in' here is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush were both US Presidents.

clue.text: Supply of firefighters late to hospital going up around noon

parts.note: H for hospital, as on road signs

indicators.note: In a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards.

parts.note: tardy means late
N for noon, placed inside HYDRAT

explanation.surface: Firefighters arrive late to a hospital fire around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal is done first: TARDY + H read upwards is HYDRAT, and then N goes inside before the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydrant supplies water to firefighters from the mains.

clue.text: One whose work attracts interest, certainly in the old City

indicators.note: One word placed in another sits inside it.

parts.note: Ur, the ancient Sumerian city
sure, as in 'sure, I'll come'

explanation.surface: A banker in the historic City of London whose work is certainly interesting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old City' suggests the City of London, Britain's financial district; it is Ur. 'Interest' is money charged on a loan, not curiosity.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at interest, traditionally excessive interest.

clue.text: Embryonic sac in mother inverted in operation

indicators.note: Something inverted is turned the other way, so the letters run backwards.

parts.note: taken as printed
ma for mother; IN + MA reversed gives AMNI
a machine in operation is on

explanation.surface: A surgeon finds an embryonic sac in the mother turned the wrong way during surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is part of the wordplay, not a link: both IN and MA are reversed together. 'Operation' reads as surgery; 'in operation' is ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The amnion is the membrane sac that encloses an embryo.

clue.text: Considered drink bottles safe

indicators.note: Something that bottles another holds it inside.

parts.note: mead is a honey drink
safe as in 'a sure bet'

explanation.surface: Someone thinks drink bottles are probably safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a plural noun beside 'drink'; it is the verb, to hold inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A measured response is considered, carefully thought out.

clue.text: Whale's skin and porpoise's covering up blubber

indicators.note: A word's covering is its outer layer, so take its first and last letters.
In a down entry, up means reading bottom to top, so the letters run backwards.
A word's skin is its outside, so take the first and last letters.

parts.note: the outer letters of WhalE
the outer letters of PorpoisE, PE, turned round

explanation.surface: A description of marine mammal anatomy: skin and an outer layer of fat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blubber' looks like the whale fat; it is the verb, to cry noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to blubber is to cry noisily and without restraint.

clue.text: Old gout remedy doctor keeps about emergency room

indicators.note: Something that keeps another holds it inside.

parts.note: to doctor an animal is to castrate it, to geld it
round, as in 'show someone round'
ER for emergency room

explanation.surface: A doctor with an old gout cure in hand rushes about the emergency room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the verb, to castrate, giving GELD, not a physician such as DR or MO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground elder, also called goutweed, was once used to treat gout.

clue.text: Blooming unruly youth going topless

indicators.note: Topless means losing the top, which in a down entry is the first letter.

parts.note: a lout is an unruly young man

explanation.surface: An exasperated remark about a wild young man stripping off his shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like a mild British swear word; it means in flower, which is what OUT means of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A gardener's sense: flowers that have opened are said to be out, that is, in bloom.

clue.text: Snake is lighter, say, without its tail

indicators.note: A word without its tail has lost its last letter.

parts.note: a lighter is a flat-bottomed barge, one kind of boat

explanation.surface: A snake is compared to a cigarette lighter lacking its end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' looks like the thing that makes a flame; it is a barge used to unload ships, and 'say' marks it as one example of a BOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: boas are large constricting snakes of the Americas.

clue.text: What fag end is put back — it will attract vermin

indicators.note: Putting something back turns it the other way round, so the letters run backwards.

parts.note: a cigarette stub is mostly filter, so it is PART TAR

explanation.surface: A dropped cigarette end is thrown back and draws in rats.
explanation.walkthrough: A fag is British slang for a cigarette. The stub's filter has soaked up tar, so it is PART TAR; read backwards, that is RAT TRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat trap is baited to lure the vermin it catches.

clue.text: River suffered without the UN

indicators.note: Without means lacking, so the named letters are removed.

parts.note: to undergo hardship is to suffer it
the United Nations, taken out of the front

explanation.surface: A river is said to have suffered from the lack of United Nations support.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derwent is a river in northern England; several English rivers share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derwent is a river in Derbyshire and elsewhere in England.
